evidence.title: Outage performance provides bounded evidence of learning after AI exposure
evidence.observation: Source-reported finding: The final journal study reports 5,172 support workers and a 15% average productivity gain. Workers exposed to AI retained faster chat handling during outages, which the authors interpret as suggestive learning. Some high-skilled workers showed small negative quality effects despite increasing adherence. Observation period and measurement context: Staggered rollout chiefly fall 2020/winter 2021; complete panel endpoints not established.
evidence.evidence_standing: Source-reported bounded account; study or measurement; not independently reproduced
evidence.glossary_fit: Illustrative or qualifying; does not validate a definition
evidence.limitations: Single firm, medium-run staggered observational adoption; outage chat duration does not measure individual-chat resolution. Outage estimates are noisy and may reflect chat mix. Does not establish durable generalized competence, long-run wages or aggregate labor demand. Data/code not independently analyzed.
evidence.open_questions: Transfer to other populations, tasks and operating environments remains unestablished. Missing measurement details are not inferred.
evidence.support_assessment: Commons interpretation: Qualifies inevitable skill decay while retaining task-specific quality costs and uncertainty.
evidence.dispute_status: See source version and dispute qualifications; no systematic clearance claimed.
evidence.verification_status: Not independently verified by the Commons

terms.name: Competency decay
terms.definition: A decline in the human or organizational expertise needed to perform, verify, contest, or recover work that is repeatedly delegated to AI-enabled systems. It is especially consequential when skills needed for independent judgment are lost.

relationships.explanation: Bounded counterevidence to inevitable decline, alongside heterogeneous quality effects.
